LLM-DEBUG-001.title: OTEL debug logging enabled — leaks prompts, thinking, tool parameters, and tool results
LLM-DEBUG-001.description: Claude Code OTEL debug-logging env vars emit sensitive content as OpenTelemetry log events / span attributes. OTEL_LOG_RAW_API_BODIES=1 (v2.1.111+) emits full request and response bodies (prompts, thinking, assistant responses). OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1 (v2.1.101+) logs tool parameters into spans — and since v2.1.157 also into tool_decision events — exposing Bash command lines, Write/Edit file paths and contents, and any secret passed as a tool argument. OTEL_LOG_TOOL_CONTENT=1 logs full tool results (file contents, command output, query results). OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS=1 emits user_system_prompt and user_prompt span/event content (full user prompts and the system prompt, plus slash-command names and sources) — direct leakage of user input and instructions. In production telemetry pipelines or any backend routed to a SaaS observability platform, enabling any of these is a confidentiality breach. Designed for local debugging only.

remediation.description: Never enable OTEL_LOG_RAW_API_BODIES, OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS, or OTEL_LOG_TOOL_CONTENT in production, CI, or any environment exporting telemetry to a shared backend — they leak prompts, tool parameters (command lines, file paths, secrets), and tool results. Use them only in local debugging with ephemeral logs. If needed for incident response, scope to a specific session via a command-line export and scrub logs immediately after. Note: Sentinel's own performance-tracing guidance uses OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1 in a trusted local/ephemeral context only — annotate such usage with `# local only`.
remediation.code_example:
# WRONG — committed to repo or CI config
OTEL_LOG_RAW_API_BODIES=1
OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1
OTEL_LOG_TOOL_CONTENT=1

# RIGHT — local debug only, ephemeral shell
$ OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1 claude --bare -p '/my-skill' 2>debug.log  # local only
$ shred -u debug.log  # scrub after

LLM-CCHARDEN-001.title: Claude Code defensive controls disabled (safe-mode / bundled-skills / idle-timeout)
LLM-CCHARDEN-001.description: Claude Code settings that weaken the agent's own security posture, dangerous when set in shared, CI, or committed environments rather than ad-hoc local troubleshooting. CLAUDE_CODE_SAFE_MODE=1 (or --safe-mode, v2.1.169+) starts Claude Code with ALL customizations disabled — CLAUDE.md, plugins, skills, hooks, and MCP servers — which silently bypasses any hook-based audit, guardrail skill, or MCP policy control. CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_BUNDLED_SKILLS=1 (or disableBundledSkills) hides bundled skills, workflows, and built-in slash commands from the model, shrinking the defensive surface. API_FORCE_IDLE_TIMEOUT=0 (v2.1.163+) disables the 5-minute idle-stream timeout, allowing indefinite stream hangs (DoS / slow data exfiltration). These belong in an ephemeral local shell, never in .env, CI config, Dockerfiles, or managed settings.

remediation.description: Never persist CLAUDE_CODE_SAFE_MODE, CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_BUNDLED_SKILLS, or API_FORCE_IDLE_TIMEOUT=0 in committed config, CI, Dockerfiles, or managed settings — they disable hooks/MCP/skill-based controls and idle-timeout protections that your security posture relies on. Use --safe-mode only as an interactive, one-off troubleshooting flag in a local shell. If a hook or MCP server misbehaves, fix or scope it rather than globally disabling all customizations. For managed deployments, enforce policy via requiredMinimumVersion and glob deny rules instead of safe-mode.
remediation.code_example:
# WRONG — committed / CI / Docker: silently disables hooks, MCP, skills
ENV CLAUDE_CODE_SAFE_MODE=1
API_FORCE_IDLE_TIMEOUT=0

# RIGHT — interactive, local, one-off troubleshooting only
$ claude --safe-mode   # then exit; never export it

LLM-CCSANDBOX-001.title: Claude Code sandbox isolation weakened (filesystem / network allowlist / credentials / Apple Events)
LLM-CCSANDBOX-001.description: Claude Code sandbox settings that reduce the isolation applied to sandboxed commands. sandbox.filesystem.disabled=true (v2.1.216+) skips filesystem isolation entirely while keeping only network egress control, so a sandboxed command regains full read/write access to the host tree. sandbox.network.strictAllowlist=false (v2.1.219+) lets sandboxed commands reach hosts that are not on the allowlist without prompting, defeating egress control and enabling silent exfiltration. sandbox.credentials configured to permit credential access lets sandboxed commands read credential files and secret environment variables (v2.1.187+ added the setting precisely to block this). sandbox.allowAppleEvents=true (v2.1.181+) lets sandboxed commands drive other macOS applications via Apple Events — a sandbox escape by proxy. Each of these is legitimate as a deliberate, scoped, local choice; committed to a repo, a Dockerfile, CI config, or managed settings, they silently strip the isolation that the rest of the posture assumes.

remediation.description: Keep sandbox isolation at its defaults in anything committed or shared. Prefer narrowing the specific permission that blocks you over disabling a whole isolation layer: add the host to the network allowlist rather than setting strictAllowlist=false; grant a specific path rather than filesystem.disabled=true. Keep sandbox.credentials blocking credential files and secret environment variables — that setting exists to stop a sandboxed command from reading what the sandbox was meant to protect. On macOS, leave allowAppleEvents off unless a named workflow requires driving a specific app, and scope it to a local session. If a setting must be relaxed temporarily, do it in an ephemeral shell and annotate it `# local only`.
